author: Barton, Craig

summary: Barton's page summarizes Slavin, Hurley, and Chamberlain's review of thirty years of cooperative-learning research, organized around four theoretical perspectives: motivational, social cohesion, and two cognitive views. The central finding is that group goals combined with individual accountability are what make cooperative learning effective; when group rewards are tied to each member's individual learning, students are motivated to teach and assess one another, and achievement rises. Methods lacking either group goals or individual accountability show weaker effects. The review also identifies contexts where these structures matter less, including higher-level cognitive tasks, voluntary study groups, and culturally grounded communal learning groups. Beyond academic achievement, cooperative learning is linked to gains in intrinsic motivation, willingness to attempt difficult tasks, higher-order thinking, and more positive attitudes toward school.
points: Group goals combined with individual accountability are the active ingredient in cooperative learning; rewarding the group based on each member's individual learning is what drives the achievement gains.
The most powerful combination is group rewards plus structured strategy training together, outperforming either element alone for math achievement in one study cited.
Higher-level cognitive tasks, voluntary study groups, and culturally grounded communal learning groups are contexts where group goals and individual accountability may matter less.
Cooperative learning's benefits extend beyond achievement to intrinsic motivation, willingness to take on difficult tasks, higher-order thinking, and more positive attitudes toward school.
quotes: This academic article reviews 30 years of research on cooperative learning in education, exploring four major theoretical perspectives: motivational, social cohesion, and two cognitive viewpoints.
Group goals and individual accountability are essential for the effectiveness of cooperative learning.
The combination of group rewards and strategy training is more effective than either one alone.
Cooperative learning has benefits beyond academic achievement. Studies show that cooperative learning can lead to positive affective and non-achievement outcomes.
Use of group goals or group rewards enhances the achievement outcomes of cooperative learning if and only if the group rewards are based on the individual learning of all group members
